transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-12
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marcus Alvarez (Redwood Solutions), Marcus Chen (Acme Platform Eng), Elena Torres (Acme ML Infra Lead), Samir Patel (Acme Security), Rita Gomez (Acme Data Eng)

Summary:
High-level technical deep dive on long-context (128k+) performance, focusing on runtime behavior, KV cache strategies, batching and chunking for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem deployment constraints. Customer is evaluating a pilot for on-prem and VPC dedicated capacity to support large-document analytics with strict latency SLOs (p95 < 500ms single-turn for summaries, streaming OK).

Topics covered:
- 128k+ context behavior and memory implications
- chunking strategies for embeddings/RAG and how Redwood routing handles it
- KV cache warmup, TTL, and eviction for long sessions
- batching, continuous batching vs immediate low-latency paths
- quantization (4-bit/8-bit) impact on throughput and quality
- on-prem/VPC network constraints, KMS/HSM integration, SOC2 implications

[00:00] Jordan Lee: okay everyone, uh thanks for joining, we've got about an hour, we wanted to do a deep dive on the 128k long context work and how it behaves on our runtime.
[00:22] Marcus Chen: thanks Jordan, yeah appreciate it. we're trying to understand tradeoffs — we have a corpus that's effectively multi-million token across docs, but typical session is like 50k to 200k tokens depending on how the user navigates.
[00:35] Priya Shah: cool, thanks Marcus. quick note, i'll surface the runtime diagrams and i'll call out the kv-cache behavior specifically, also we'll show how chunking plus caching reduces recompute across the i/o path.
[00:50] Elena Torres: our big constraints: 1) we want predictable latency for single-turn summary requests, 2) cost matters but we'll pay for dedicated if latency is stable, and 3) we have strict network egress rules — on-prem preferable.
[01:05] Jordan Lee: got it. quick baseline — with Atlas-128k-ish models we see two main bottlenecks: attention memory growth (quadratic-ish in naive attention) and kv-cache memory / lookup overhead once you get to hundreds of thousands of tokens. on top of that quantization and kernel choice matter a lot for throughput.
[01:28] Samir Patel: when you say Atlas, do you mean Redwood-Atlas or a community model? we need licensing and security info.
[01:34] Jordan Lee: yes Redwood-Atlas-128k is our verified variant; we can also run open models. i'll share the list and licensing notes after — we'll include SOC2 docs and our model catalog.
[01:45] [00:60] Priya Shah: jumping in — on the runtime side: our serving runtime does continuous batching but we also expose a low-latency pipeline that bypasses some batching for p95-sensitive calls. for 128k use we tend to recommend a hybrid: small immediate batch path for the first N tokens and then a higher-throughput path when you stream or do long autoregressive spans.
[02:10] Rita Gomez: how does that hybrid work with RAG? we chunk documents and embed them, but when you reconstruct context you sometimes end up overlapping chunks and you're worried about double-counting.
[02:25] Priya Shah: good question. we recommend deterministic chunking with overlap tuned (10-20%) and then use a prefix normalization step before feeding into the model; the KV cache is keyed per-prefix so repeated prefixes reuse cached KV frames, which reduces compute. but the cache efficiency depends on how similar queries are and your chunking granularity.
[02:44] Marcus Alvarez: what's the warmup cost for the KV cache? if i have a burst of 100 users each with 100k tokens, do we have to recompute a ton?
[02:53] Priya Shah: warmup depends on cache TTL and your shard sizing. example: on a 4-GPU pool with 80GB each, we can keep X gigabytes of kv entries — cold start is expensive but our routing supports staged warmups and prefetching. for repeated queries across users the shared prefixes yield big wins. we also support pre-warming via a small upfront batch job.
[03:15] Elena Torres: and for on-prem, is that pre-warm job something we run? or does Redwood manage it in Dedicated?
[03:22] Jordan Lee: for private deployments, Redwood provides automation scripts for pre-warm and a config to run scheduled warmup jobs; for Dedicated/hosted we can run it for you.
[03:30] [03:35] Samir Patel: on encryption — for KV cache data at rest, how do you handle KMS? we cannot have unencrypted mem-mapped files.
[03:42] Priya Shah: we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key wrapping. KV frames in memory are ephemeral, but persisted checkpoints are encrypted. for strict requirements we can put an additional encryption layer and FIPS-approved modules if needed. we'll include our network and KMS diagram in the follow-up.
[04:00] Jordan Lee: moving to batching and latency: tradeoff chart — small batch sizes reduce latency but hurt throughput; large batches are great for throughput but p95 will increase. the sweet spot depends on your percent of streaming vs single-turn. for 128k contexts if you're doing summarization of large doc, you often chunk and run multiple shorter decodes in parallel then stitch results to reduce p95.
[04:30] [04:48] Rita Gomez: stitching — is that done client side? we have concerns about state consistency and alignment.
[04:52] Priya Shah: we provide helpers to stitch deterministic chunks server-side, including token offsets and metadata so you can reconcile. you can also stream partials and do final merge client-side.
[05:10] Marcus Chen: quantization — how much does 4-bit hurt quality for long context? we tested off-the-shelf and saw hallucination spikes.
[05:20] Priya Shah: yep — 4-bit can reduce model expressivity in edge cases. our recommendation: start with 8-bit (QAT or quant aware kernels) for long-context production; use 4-bit for heavy throughput where you can accept a small drop. we have per-workload evals and can run a small regression suite; we'll show example tradeoffs in the spreadsheet.
[05:42] Jordan Lee: another lever is selective quantization — quantize attention/weights differently than embeddings; on some kernels we can keep certain layers in higher precision to preserve quality while saving memory elsewhere.
[05:55] [06:10] Priya Shah: attention optimizations — we use chunked attention kernels and fused rotary/ALiBi where appropriate; that reduces memory overhead and improves throughput for very long sequences. also we have a method for attention-sparsification for retrieval-heavy prompts which prunes attention to recent windows and retrieved chunk anchors.
[06:35] Elena Torres: can we see numbers? like 128k end-to-end latency for a 2-pass summarize vs naive single-pass?
[06:44] Priya Shah: short answer: naive single-pass at 128k with full attention is usually impractical for real-time. our two-pass approach (local chunk-level summarize then final aggregate) tends to reduce p95 by 3-5x depending on chunk size. i'll attach a benchmark example — e.g., with 8-bit kernels and chunking to 4k windows we saw per-user p95 go from ~3.2s to ~0.9s in our internal tests for similar workloads.
[07:15] Marcus Chen: those numbers look promising. what's the GPU footprint? if we want to run 50 concurrent users with 128k-ish sessions, are we looking at dedicated 8xA100s or something else?
[07:26] Jordan Lee: depends; for throughput-heavy batch workloads you can multiplex more sessions per GPU with quantization and larger batch sizes. for low-latency p95 targets you'd provision more nodes. as a rule of thumb, 50 concurrent long-context interactive sessions with p95 < 500ms typically maps to an 8-GPU pool with sizing tuned — we'll run a sizing exercise for your corpus.
[07:45] [08:00] Samir Patel: network egress — for private we need no egress to public internet. can Redwood run the control plane outside while the runtime is fully in our VPC?
[08:08] Jordan Lee: yes our Private deployment supports a customer-managed control plane with optional air-gapped runtime. you can choose fully private control plane or split model where telemetry is limited. we'll share our deployment modes and SSO/SAML integration notes.
[08:28] Priya Shah: another gotcha is pinned model versions and rollouts — for experimentation you might want canarying. our rollout engine supports rolling A/B on Dedicated and Private with automatic fallback to lower-capacity variants if a node fails.
[08:43] Rita Gomez: about tooling — how do we debug KV cache misses and hot prefixes?
[08:48] Priya Shah: the console exposes per-prefix hit rates, token-level cost breakdowns, and trace hooks. we'll enable a dev dashboard for you in the pilot.
[09:00] [09:10] Marcus Chen: what about chunk overlap and retrieval duplicates — sometimes the same sentence appears in multiple chunks and the model repeats. any heuristics?
[09:18] Priya Shah: yes we apply dedupe heuristics at the embedding/retrieval layer and a normalization pass before final decode. for redundancy we also recommend lower overlap (10%) for retrieval-heavy and higher overlap for semantic continuity.
[09:36] Jordan Lee: wrap up with pilot plan — propose a staged pilot: 1) small on-prem test with 1-2 nodes and 128k dataset subset to validate latency/quality, 2) expanded stress test to measure concurrency and KV cache behavior, 3) integrate KMS and networking checks, 4) run evals and quality regression.
[09:58] Elena Torres: timeline — we can do stage 1 next week if you send the config and scripts.
[10:03] Jordan Lee: yes we'll send the scripts.
